profiles.meeting_scenario: An asset management firm's research planning meeting for turning a new academic paper on growth-optimal portfolios under transaction costs into a client-facing internal prototype. The team wants to decide what will be built over the next three weeks: a planning memo, a backtest demonstration, and a short slide deck for the firm's multi-asset investment committee. The meeting context is that the CIO asked for something 'practical enough to review this month' after reading a summary of the paper. The agenda is to define the prototype scope, decide what counts as a usable demonstration, assign modeling vs implementation responsibilities, and set an end-of-month timeline. The expected outcome is an agreed plan for a prototype that appears aligned around a Markovian transaction-cost-aware portfolio model, a committee-ready demo, and ownership of the work.

members.name: Elena Park
members.expertise: systematic investing, portfolio construction, academic-to-production research translation
members.background: Elena leads the firm's quantitative research incubation work and previously spent six years at a global macro fund adapting academic allocation models into committee-ready research notes.
members.private_state: She wants a polished prototype that can persuade the investment committee the idea is strategically important without exposing the team to criticism for weak implementation details; she is especially concerned about producing something that looks too toy-like.
hidden_assumptions: A 'prototype' for committee review should include a realistic backtest with turnover frictions and operationally plausible rebalancing constraints, even if some theoretical details are simplified.
When someone says 'transaction costs' in a portfolio-planning context, that naturally includes market-impact-style trading frictions and minimum trade thresholds, not just broker fee terms.

A 'Markovian implementation' means the allocation rule conditions on a compact state of current holdings plus a few estimated economic regime variables derived from the firm's existing macro state engine.
If a deliverable is due 'by month-end,' it should be ready for circulation before the committee packet freeze at 3 p.m. New York time on the last business day.
The backtest can rely on the firm's standard monthly total-return panel and factor regime labels because those are the default research inputs unless someone explicitly says otherwise.

members.name: Victor Shah
members.expertise: research infrastructure, backtesting systems, portfolio simulation pipelines
members.background: Victor manages the internal quant platform team and previously built execution-aware portfolio simulators for a broker-dealer's institutional strategy group.
members.private_state: He wants a narrowly scoped build that his team can deliver reliably with existing infrastructure, and he is wary of open-ended research requests that quietly become bespoke production asks.
hidden_assumptions: A 'prototype' in this setting means a reproducible research harness that demonstrates the paper's mechanism, not a committee-polished investment study.
When someone says 'transaction costs,' the natural reading for this paper translation is the explicit fixed-plus-proportional fee schedule from the paper, implemented literally in the simulator.

A 'Markovian implementation' means the policy uses only variables present in the simulation state at time t, especially current weights and the externally supplied factor state, without additional estimated regime overlays.
If something is needed 'by month-end,' the commitment is code and outputs checked into the research repository by end of day UTC on the last calendar day.

The relevant data for a first pass is the daily cleaned equities-and-ETF sandbox already connected to the backtest engine, because using the firm's macro regime engine would require extra integration work that would have been mentioned explicitly if needed.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to deliver a 'prototype' for the investment committee.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes the prototype must look committee-ready: a credible backtest, practical constraints, summary exhibits, and a narrative strong enough for strategic review.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes the prototype only needs to prove the concept in the research stack: runnable code, a baseline simulation, and basic output tables showing the mechanism works.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In business planning meetings, 'prototype' is a positively valenced, familiar term that sounds aligned; both think their interpretation is standard and neither sees a reason to unpack the quality bar unless problems emerge later.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the model should include 'transaction costs' consistent with the paper.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a practical cost layer including fixed ticket costs, proportional fees, and de facto trading frictions such as minimum-trade thresholds and simple market-impact penalties to avoid unrealistic turnover.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the simulator should implement only the paper's explicit fixed-plus-proportional cost structure and no extra frictions unless separately specified.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'transaction costs' appears to be shared technical language, and because the paper itself mentions fixed plus proportional costs, each person assumes the other naturally maps that phrase onto their own customary extension of the term.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to build a 'Markovian version' of the strategy using economic factors.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 expects the strategy to use the firm's existing monthly macro regime labels and current holdings, treating those regime indicators as the practical economic-factor state.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 expects to use only factor-state fields already available inside the daily simulation sandbox, with no dependency on the firm's separate macro regime engine or monthly aggregation workflow.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: They agree on the high-level method and both mention 'economic factors' and 'Markovian,' so the hidden divergence is in the execution path and source of state variables, which feels too implementation-adjacent and too obvious to either of them to spell out.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the first version will be ready 'by month-end.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this means materials are polished and circulated internally before the committee packet cutoff at 3 p.m. New York time on the last business day of the month.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this means repository code and output files are available by 11:59 p.m. UTC on the last calendar day of the month.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Month-end sounds like a shared organizational deadline, but each member silently anchors it to the scheduling norms of their own function—committee operations for M1 and engineering delivery conventions for M2.

turns.inner_thought: The CIO wants something practical enough to survive committee scrutiny, not a lab demo. If we call it a prototype, it has to look credible: a realistic backtest, sensible constraints, and transaction costs that don't make the path look naive. And 'by month-end' means before packet freeze on the last business day, not some engineering timestamp after everyone's gone home.
